title: Cōḻaṉ
paragraphs: Ten years ago, an old woman was seen staggering with a stick on the bank of the Koḷḷiṭam river, being unable to walk with an upright gait due to scorching heat. A cowherd youth sitting under a tree took pity upon the ageing woman and approached her with some fruits. The youth held her famished hands and enquired, “Grandmother! Where are you going in this hot sun? You are hardly able to walk. Here, have these fruits.” He offered the blackberries to her.
The old woman scrutinized the fruits carefully and remarked rather mockingly, “Are these fruits hot or cold?”
“The aged don’t lose their sense of humour, do they? I am no Lord Murukaṉ. First, have these fruits!”
The old woman tasted the fruits, touched the shoulders of the youth affectionately and questioned, “Son! Why are you rearing cows at this age instead of going to school?”.
“Well! I am studying. I do this work only during holidays.”
“Is there nobody at home?”
“My father is afflicted with tuberculosis. When I go to school, my mother rears the cows and milks them to make our both ends meet.”
“It is quite pathetic! How do you concentrate upon your education, amid such gruelling poverty? What are you studying and what do you want to become?”
“I am studying Tamil. My ambition is to work as a Tamil teacher!”
“Is it so? Quite good! Is your Tamil teacher tutoring you in literature?”
“Oh yes! He is teaching Tirukkuṟaḷ, Tolkāppiyam and all.”
“In that case, I know a little of literature, as I happen to be a retired Tamil teacher. I would ask you a question. Would you answer?”
“Please do ask, grandmother. I will answer!”
“Suppose I say that Cōḻaṉ would come (varum) to take me, is Cōḻaṉ here human or non-human class?”
“Grandmother, if Cōḻaṉ referred to by you happens to be your son or grandson, it is human! In case Cōḻaṉ points to the bus, it is non-human class.”
“Son, how do you say so? What is its grammatical explanation?”
“Grandmother, look! Tolkāppiyam’s Eḻuttatikāram is crystal clear in this regard:
> There is non-change coalescence too > Where > Nouns that designate > Both the human and non-human generic classes > Are the preceding words.
The noun that takes both human and non-human classes is called a common noun. That is how my explanation holds good. The human masculine Cōḻaṉ normally becomes non-human.”

“Dear grandson! You are more talented than Lord Murukaṉ himself who proved his mettle before Avvai, in those days. While he demonstrated his Tamil proficiency only with regard to a fruit, you have revealed your talent in age-old Tamil grammar. May you flourish in your life! May you flourish in your life!”
The Cōḻaṉ came (vantuviṭṭāṉ) during the shower of greetings. No, no, it came (vantuviṭṭatu). The old lady planted a kiss upon the forehead of the youth and boarded the bus with his assistance.
> There is non-change coalescence too > Where > Nouns that designate > Both the human and non-human generic classes > Are the preceding words. > > (Eḻuttatikāram : Tokaimarapu, verse 13)
